Τῶν κινουμένων τὰ μέν τινα ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἔχει τὴν τῆς κινήσεως αἰτίαν, ἕτερα δὲ ἔξωϑεν μόνον κινεῖται. ἔξωϑεν μὲν οὖν μόνον κινεῖται τὰ φορητά, οἷον ξύλα καὶ λίϑοι καὶ πᾶσα ἡ ὑπὸ ἕξεως μόνης συνεχομένη ὕλη. ὑπεξηῃηρήσϑω δὲ νῦν τοῦ λόγου τὸ κίνησιν λέγειν τὴν δύσιν τῶν σωμάτων, ἐπεὶ μὴ χρεία τούτου πρὸς τὸ προκείμενον. ἐν ξαυτοῖς δὲ ἔχει τὴν αἰτίαν τοῦ κινεῖσϑαι ζῷα καὶ φυτὰ καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς ὅσα ὑπὸ φύσεως ἢ ψυχῆς συνέχεται: ἐξ ὧν φασιν εἶναι xci τὰ μέταλλα, πρὸς δὲ τούτοις καὶ τὸ πῦρ αὐτοκίνητόν ἐστι, τάχα δὲ καὶ αἱ πηγαί. τῶν δὲ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς τὴν αἰτίαν τοῦ κινεῖσϑαι ἐχοντῶν τὰ μέν φασιν ἐξ ἑαυτῶν χινεῖσϑαι, τὰ δὲ ἀφ᾽ ξαυτῶν" ἐξ ξαυτῶν μὲν τὰ ἄψυχα, ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῶν δὲ τὰ ἔμψυχα. καὶ ἀφ᾽ ξαυτῶν xiνεῖται τὰ ἔμψυχα, φαντασίας ἐγγινομένης ὁρμὴν προκαλουμένης. xal πάλιν Ev τισι τῶν ζῴων φαντασίαι γίνονται ὁρμὴν προ καλούμεναι, φύσεως φανταστικῆς τεταγμένως κινούσης τὴν ὁρμήν, ος ἐν τῷ ἀράχνῃ φαντασία τοῦ ὑφαίνειν γίνεται καὶ ὁρμὴ ἀκολουϑεῖ ἐπὶ τὸ ὑφαίνειν, τῆς φανταστικῆς αὐτοῦ φύσεως τεταγμένως ἐπὶ τοῦτο αὐτὸν προκαλουμένης xal οὐδενὸς ἄλλου μετὰ τὴν φανταστικὴν αὖτοῦ φύσιν πεπιστευμένου τοῦ ζῴου, καὶ ἐν τῇ μελίσσῃ ἐπὶ τὸ χηροσπλαστεῖν. 3(2). pass_a_gloss: He will say in the ecclesiastical preaching that the word about the righteous anointing of God is contained, which, being believed to be true, also provokes to living well and fleeing from sin in every way, so that we may privately take the most necessary problem, namely that we have it. And so that we may understand what the self-moved is, it is necessary to unfold the notion of it, so that with it having been clarified, what is sought may be precisely presented. For of the things being moved, some have the cause of the movement in themselves, but others are moved only from outside. The things being carried, such as wood and stones and all matter that is held together only by habit, are moved only from outside. But let the word about the movement of bodies be left out for now, since it is not necessary for the present subject. And animals and plants and all things that are held together by nature or soul have the cause of being moved in themselves: from which they say metals are, and besides these, fire is self-moved, and perhaps also springs. And of the things having the cause of being moved in themselves, some are said to be moved from themselves, but others from outside themselves: the non-living from outside themselves, but the living from themselves. And the living are moved from themselves, a fantasy occurring and provoking an impulse. And again, in some of the animals, fantasies occur provoking an impulse, nature having arranged the fantasy to move the impulse, as in the spider, a fantasy of weaving occurs and an impulse follows to weave, the fantasy of its nature having arranged it to this very thing, and no other thing being believed by the animal after its fantasy, and in the bee to shape wax. But the rational animal also has reason in relation to its fantasy nature, approving some fantasies and rejecting others, so that the animal may be led according to them. Whence, since in the nature of reason there are starting points to consider the good and the bad, following which, having considered the good and the bad, we choose the good and turn away from the bad, we are praiseworthy when we give ourselves to the practice of the good, but blameworthy according to the opposite. It should not be unknown, however, that the greater part of nature that is arranged in all things is in the animals, and for the most part or for the lesser part, so that it is near, I say, the work of the rational in the tracking dogs and in the war horses. For the thing that is submitted to from outside, a fantasy moving us in such and such a way, is admittedly not in our power: but to judge whether to use what has happened in such and such a way or otherwise, is the work of our reason, either working in us according to the starting points that provoke us to the good and to duty, or turning us away to the opposite.

pass_b_english: He will declare in the church's preaching that the message concerning God's righteous anointing is contained there, and this message, once believed true, urges people to live well and to flee sin in every way, precisely so that we may take up for ourselves the most necessary problem—that we possess it. In order to understand what the self-moved is, one must develop its concept, so that once it is clarified, the question at hand may be set forth precisely. Of things that move, some have the cause of their motion within themselves, while others are moved only from outside. Objects that are carried—such as wood, stones, and all matter held together solely by habit—are moved only from outside. Let the discussion of bodily motion be set aside for now, since it is not needed for the present subject. Animals and plants, and in general all things held together by nature or soul, have the cause of their motion within themselves; some say metals belong to this group, and in addition fire is self-moved, and perhaps springs as well. Among things that have the cause of motion in themselves, some are said to be moved from themselves, others from outside themselves: the non-living from outside themselves, the living from themselves. The living are moved from themselves when a fantasy occurs and provokes an impulse. Again, in some animals fantasies arise that provoke an impulse, with nature having arranged the fantasy so as to move the impulse in a fixed way, as in the spider a fantasy of weaving occurs and an impulse follows to weave, its fantasy nature having arranged it for this very thing, with no other thing believed by the animal after its fantasy, and in the bee for shaping wax. The rational animal, however, also possesses reason alongside its fantasy nature, reason that evaluates fantasies, rejecting some and accepting others, so that the animal may be led according to them. Since there are starting points in the nature of reason for contemplating the good and the bad, by following them we contemplate the good and the bad, choose the good and turn away from the bad; we are praiseworthy when we give ourselves to practicing the good, blameworthy when we do the opposite. It must not be overlooked, however, that the greater part of the nature ordered in all things exists quantitatively in animals, and for the most part or for the lesser part, so that it is near, one might say, the work of the rational in tracking dogs and war horses. Submitting to something external that moves a fantasy in us this way or that is admittedly not in our power; but to judge whether to use what has occurred in this way or otherwise is the work of the reason within us, whether it operates in us according to the starting points that urge us toward the good and toward duty, or turns us away toward the opposite.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, particularly the distinction between internal and external causes of motion and the role of reason in evaluating fantasies. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek source. The title 'Free Will' correctly identifies the thought of the passage regarding the 'αὐτεξούσιον' (the power of self-determination/agency).
